c.v: Without looking anything up, write two lists. First, every QoS policy that can stop a publisher and a subscription from connecting at all, and for each one the combination that fails. Second, the policies that never stop a connection but do change what you receive, and what each of them changes. Take 10 minutes.
Four policies can stop a connection, and the rule behind all four is the same. A subscription
the lowest quality it will accept and a publisher
the highest quality it can provide, and the pair is matched only when the offer is at least as strong as the request, policy by policy.

items.v: Reliability: a best-effort publisher against a reliable subscription fails. Reliable against best effort is fine, and so are the two matching pairs.
Durability: a volatile publisher against a transient-local subscription fails. Transient local against volatile is fine.
Deadline: a publisher with no deadline against a subscription that asks for one fails, and so does a subscription whose deadline is shorter than the publisher's. Longer or equal is fine.

Liveliness: an automatic publisher against a subscription that asks for manual by topic fails. A publisher with no lease duration against a subscription that asks for one fails, and so does a shorter requested lease.

c.v: The policies that never break a connection are history, depth and lifespan. History and depth size each side's own queue, so a depth of 1 on one side and 100 on the other connect and drop different messages. Lifespan is the publisher's own expiry: a message older than the lifespan is dropped before delivery and is never seen, with no warning.

You pass if you named reliability and durability with the right failing direction and at least one of deadline and liveliness, and put history and depth in the second list. Naming the policies but getting a direction backwards is a partial pass. Putting depth in the first list is a fail, because it leads to hours spent matching queue sizes that were never the problem.

A QoS profile is the set of delivery promises every publisher and every subscription carries. Reliability says what happens to a message the network drops: best effort sends it once and moves on, reliable keeps a copy until it is acknowledged and resends it if not. Durability says what a subscription starting late receives: volatile gives it nothing sent before it joined, transient local replays what the publisher has kept. Deadline promises the longest gap between messages, and liveliness is how a subscription learns a publisher is still there.

The problem is that a publisher and a subscription must agree on these promises before a single message can flow, and getting that agreement wrong produces no error, no crash and no line in the topic listing to say so. Two nodes can find each other perfectly and still never exchange one message, because finding each other and agreeing to talk are different things.

The rule is one sentence: a subscription requests the lowest quality it will accept, a publisher offers the highest quality it can provide, and the two connect only when the offer is at least as strong as the request, policy by policy, for reliability, durability, deadline and liveliness. A stronger publisher always satisfies a weaker subscription, never the reverse, so a reliable publisher happily serves a best-effort subscriber but not the other way round. History, depth and lifespan never block a connection: they size each side's own queue or expire the publisher's own samples, changing what arrives without ever deciding whether anything can.

The costly mistake is a best-effort driver, using the sensor-data profile most drivers use, met by a reliable subscription, the default every tutorial writes: the two never connect, the topic still shows up in every listing, and the rate tools still report data because they subscribe with their own best-effort profile regardless of yours. Nothing in your own node's log has to say why, because that warning only prints while the node is spinning, and some middleware does not raise it at all. The only way to be sure is reading both endpoints' profiles side by side, not waiting for a warning that might never come.

This is the interview question itself: naming, from memory, exactly which policies can stop a connection and in which direction, and which ones only change what arrives once a connection is already made.

subs.title: Reliability, durability, history, depth, deadline, liveliness

c.v: Every publisher and every subscription carries a QoS profile, and the middleware carries it across during discovery, which is why you can read another process's settings from the command line:

blocks.text:
ros2 topic info /scan --verbose   # per endpoint: node name, GID, topic type hash and the full QoS profile
ros2 topic echo /scan             # matches what the publishers offer unless you pass a --qos-* option
ros2 doctor --report              # its QOS COMPATIBILITY LIST section names the mismatched pairs it can see

c.v: The first command is the one to reach for. For every publisher and every subscription on the topic it prints

chooses what happens to a message the network loses. Best effort sends it once and forgets it. Reliable makes the publisher keep a copy until the subscription acknowledges it, and resend it if it does not, which costs memory in the publisher, a return path on the network and latency on the retry. Both run over UDP in DDS; reliable is not TCP, it is acknowledgement and retransmission built on top of UDP so that multicast stays possible.

chooses what a subscription that starts later gets. Volatile means nothing that was sent before it joined. Transient local means the publisher keeps its history and delivers it to each new subscription that also asks for transient local. This is how ROS 2 does the latched topic of ROS 1, and it is why a map or a robot description published once at start-up still reaches a node started five minutes later. The publisher has to be alive for it: what transient local stores lives in the publisher, not in a broker, so when the publishing process exits the stored samples go with it.

size the queue. Keep last with depth N holds the newest N messages per publisher and per subscription and drops older ones to make room; keep all holds as many as the middleware's own resource limits allow. Depth is a queue length, not a rate and not a guarantee: it decides how much slack there is when the reader falls behind, which the executors topic measured, and nothing else. Keep last with depth 0 is a mistake rclcpp logs once, with
A zero depth with KEEP_LAST doesn't make sense; no data could be stored. This will be interpreted as SYSTEM_DEFAULT

is a contract about the gap between messages, in both directions. A publisher offering a deadline of 100 ms promises to publish at least that often; a subscription requesting 100 ms says it needs that. When the promise is broken, the publisher's
event fire, each with a total count and the change since last time. A deadline is a watchdog, not a rate limiter: it never slows a publisher down and never drops a message.
is the publisher's expiry date on its own samples. A message older than the lifespan is dropped instead of delivered, with no event and no log line.
uses a lifespan of 10 seconds so that a late-joining log viewer gets recent lines and not the whole history.

is how a subscription learns that a publisher is still there. Automatic means the middleware treats all of a participant's publishers as alive whenever any one of them publishes. Manual by topic means a publisher must say so itself, by publishing or by calling the publisher's assert method, within the lease duration. Missing the lease fires
on the subscription. Automatic with no lease is the default everywhere in ROS 2, which means liveliness is switched off in practice until you ask for it.

Now the rule that ties the policies together. Compatibility is decided per publisher and subscription pair, at discovery time, by

What you see when that happens depends on your middleware. rclcpp installs a default handler for the incompatible-QoS event on every publisher and subscription, and the subscription's version logs

Here are the compatibility rules as code, in the order
checks them, run over the pairs you actually meet:

c.v: Three readings of the table. The two connecting rows in the middle say something that surprises people: a stronger publisher always serves a weaker subscription, so a reliable publisher feeds a best-effort subscriber and a transient-local publisher feeds a volatile one. You never have to weaken a publisher to reach a subscriber. The direction that fails is always the subscription asking for more than the publisher promised.
Second, deadline and lease read backwards from the others. A shorter requested duration is a stronger demand, so
is the failure, and "no value" counts as infinite, which is the weakest offer and the weakest demand at once. A publisher with no deadline can serve a subscription with no deadline and nothing else.

Third, the last row is why the rmw function returns a list rather than a flag: two policies are wrong at once, and the warning rclcpp logs names only the last one it found. Fixing the policy in the message and finding it still broken is normal, and it is the reason to read the whole profile from

subs.title: Sensor-data QoS versus reliable; late joiners

c.v: The most common QoS failure in robotics has a fixed shape. A driver publishes

reports 10 Hz, and your callback never runs. Both nodes log one warning at the moment of discovery, and that single line disappears in a launch file's output, which is why the first thing to do with a silent subscription is
and a look at the two

The cure is to decide the profile from the data, not from the habit. Anything that streams and whose newest sample is the one that matters, such as scans, images, point clouds and odometry, is sensor data on both sides. Anything that is stated once and must not be lost, such as a map, a robot description or a mode, is reliable and transient local on both sides. Commands are reliable with a depth of 1. When you do not own the publisher, read its profile and match it.
Late joiners bring the second shape. Transient local needs both ends to ask for it, so a node that subscribes to
with a profile of its own and no
misses every static transform, and the lookups then fail with an extrapolation error that says nothing about QoS. It also needs the publisher's depth to be large enough: a
storing depth 1 delivers the last sample only, which is right for one map and wrong for a topic where several different messages must all survive, such as
with more than one broadcaster. tf2 sizes its static listener at depth 100 for that reason, while its broadcaster keeps depth 1 because it republishes the whole set in one message.
Three quieter failures are worth knowing before they cost you a day.

Lifespan drops messages with no event at all. A publisher with a lifespan of 1 second and a consumer that blocks for 2 seconds in a callback gets nothing when it returns, and there is no counter anywhere to say why. If you set a lifespan, set it longer than the worst callback time you are willing to accept.

Deadline is a promise that stock drivers do not make. A subscription that asks for a 200 ms deadline will not connect to any publisher that left its deadline at the default, which is every publisher in the standard packages. So the deadline policy is useful between two nodes you wrote and useless as a watchdog on somebody else's driver, where a freshness check on the node's clock is the tool.
